clinician.final_diagnosis: MFS-GBS overlap syndrome associated with the Oxford-AstraZeneca SARS-CoV2 vaccination
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 63-year-old man with no prior medical history presented 14 days following his first dose of Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccination. He developed lower back pain 9 days post-vaccination, followed 5 days later (day 14 post-vaccination) by acute onset over 48 hours of bilateral facial weakness, unsteadiness, lower limb weakness, and paraesthesia. On admission neurological examination, he demonstrated profound sensory ataxia, facial diplegia with incomplete eye closure bilaterally, proximal lower limb weakness, bilateral lower limb areflexia, and impaired distal proprioception, unable to walk without assistance. CSF analysis revealed albuminocytologic dissociation with markedly elevated protein (2.99 g/L) and minimal cells, consistent with demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy. Serum anti-GQ1b antibody was negative. EMG/NCS showed long-standing axonal neuropathy with chronic neurogenic changes but no acute demyelination. MRI brain demonstrated bilateral enhancement of facial and oculomotor nerves, confirming facial diplegia and partial bilateral cranial nerve III palsies. The patient was treated with a 5-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) and supportive care including eye care and catheterization for urinary retention. He underwent 4 weeks of inpatient rehabilitation. At 6 weeks post-symptom onset, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia had resolved with minimal residual bilateral facial weakness and persistent proximal lower limb weakness (MRC grade 4). He returned home, living independently and ambulating with a four-wheel frame.
